note.explanation: Science studies the natural world through observation, investigation, and evidence. Physics is a physical science concerned with matter, energy, and their interactions. Scientific ideas are tested: a hypothesis is a possible answer to a question, while a theory is a well-supported explanation and a law describes a regular pattern in nature. Scientific knowledge can change when new evidence requires a theory or law to be modified.
examples: Observing that a plant near a window grows towards the light is an observation.
A prediction might be: if the plant receives more light, it will grow faster.
note.checkAnswer: A hypothesis is a possible answer to a question that can be tested.
note.simple: Science is a way of learning about nature by asking questions and checking ideas with evidence.
note.title: Nature of Science
steps: Ask a question about something you observe.
Make a prediction from the hypothesis.
Test the prediction through investigation or an experiment.
Use the evidence to support, reject, or modify the hypothesis.
note.answer: Science is the systematic study of the natural world using observation, investigation, and evidence.

mcqs.stem:
Q9.1. Physics is a branch of:
(a) social science (b) life science (c) physical science (d) biological science
rationales: Social science studies human society, not the physical world studied by Physics.
Life science focuses on living organisms rather than the main subject area of Physics.
Physics is a branch of physical science.
Biological science studies living things, so it is not the branch to which Physics belongs.

mcqs.stem:
Q9.2. Which branch of science plays vital role in technology and engineering?
(a) Biology (b) Chemistry (c) Geology (d) Physics
rationales: Biology is important in fields such as medicine, but it is not the intended answer here.
Chemistry contributes to technology, but the question asks for the branch with a vital role across technology and engineering.
Geology studies Earth and is not the intended general basis for technology and engineering.
Physics provides principles used widely in technology and engineering.

mcqs.stem:
Q9.3. Automobile technology is based on:
(a) acoustics (b) electromagnetism
(c) optics (d) thermodynamics
rationales: Acoustics concerns sound and is not the intended basis of automobile technology.
Electromagnetism is used in some vehicle systems, but it is not the intended answer.
Optics concerns light and is not the intended basis of automobile technology.
Thermodynamics concerns heat and energy transformations and is the intended answer.

mcqs.stem:
Q9.4. A user friendly software application of smart phone use:
(a) laser technology (b) information technology
(c) medical technology (d) electronic technology
rationales: Laser technology uses lasers and does not best describe smartphone software applications.
Information technology includes software applications used on smartphones.
Medical technology is technology for medical purposes, not the general software application described.
Electronic technology relates to electronic devices, but the software application is best classified as information technology.

mcqs.stem:
Q9.5. The working of refrigeration and air conditioning involves:
(a) electromagnetism (b) mechanics
(c) climate science (d) thermodynamics
rationales: Electromagnetism can be involved in device components, but it is not the intended principle.
Mechanics concerns motion and forces, not the main heat-transfer principle asked about.
Climate science studies climate and is not the operating principle of these devices.
Thermodynamics explains heat transfer and energy changes in refrigeration and air conditioning.

mcqs.stem:
Q9.6. What is the ultimate truth of a scientific method?
(a) Hypothesis (b) Experimentation
(c) Theory (d) Law
rationales: A hypothesis is a proposed answer that requires testing, not the intended answer.
Experimentation is a method of testing ideas, not the final choice in this question.
A theory is a well-supported explanation, but the book's intended answer here is a law.
A law is the intended answer among the choices.

mcqs.stem:
Q9.7. The statement "If I do not study for this test, then I will not get good grade" is an example of:
(a) theory (b) observation
(c) prediction (d) law
rationales: A theory is a supported explanation, not a statement about an expected outcome in this situation.
An observation reports something noticed, whereas this statement says what is expected to happen.
This is a prediction because it states an expected result based on a condition.
A law describes a regular pattern in nature, not this personal expected outcome.

mcqs.stem:
Q9.8. Which of the following are methods of investigation?
(a) Observation (b) Experimentation
(c) Research (d) All of these
rationales: Observation is a method of investigation, but it is not the only one listed.
Experimentation is a method of investigation, but it is not the only one listed.
Research is a method of investigation, but it is not the only one listed.
Observation, experimentation, and research are all methods of investigation.

options: may or may not be testable
is a possible answer to a question
mcqs.stem:
Q9.9. A hypothesis:
(a) may or may not be testable (b) is supported by evidence
(c) is a possible answer to a question (d) all of these
rationales: This describes the possibility that a proposed hypothesis may not yet be testable.
Evidence can support a hypothesis after it is investigated.
A hypothesis is a possible answer to a question.
The book's intended choice combines the listed descriptions of a hypothesis.

mcqs.stem:
Q9.10. A graph of an organized data is an example of:
(a) collecting data (b) forming a hypothesis
(c) asking question (d) analyzing data
rationales: Collecting data means obtaining observations or measurements, not displaying organized data as a graph.
A graph is not the formation of a proposed answer to a question.
A graph does not itself represent the act of asking a question.
Organizing and presenting data in a graph is part of analysing data.

written.text: Q9.1. State in your own words, what is science? Write its two main groups.
written.finalAnswer: Science is the systematic study of the natural world using observation and evidence. Its two main groups are physical science and life science.

rubric.why: The answer must show what science studies and how it gains knowledge.
rubric.how: State that science studies the natural world systematically using investigation or evidence.

rubric.why: The question explicitly asks for the two main groups.
rubric.how: Write physical science and life science.

modelAnswer: Science is the systematic study of the natural world using observation and evidence.
Its two main groups are physical science and life science.

written.text: Q9.2. What is Physics all about? Name some of its branches.
written.finalAnswer: Physics is the study of matter, energy, and their interactions. Its branches include mechanics, heat, sound, light, and electricity and magnetism.

rubric.why: This states the central subject matter of Physics.
rubric.how: Mention matter, energy, and their interactions.

rubric.why: Examples show knowledge of the branches of Physics.
rubric.how: Give at least two relevant branches.

modelAnswer: Physics is the study of matter, energy, and their interactions.
Its branches include mechanics, heat, sound, light, and electricity and magnetism.

written.text: Q9.4. List the main steps of scientific method.
written.finalAnswer: The main steps are asking a question, forming a hypothesis, making a prediction, testing it through investigation or experimentation, collecting and analysing data, and drawing a conclusion.

rubric.why: These are the initial steps that guide an investigation.
rubric.how: Include a question, hypothesis, and prediction.

rubric.why: Testing and interpreting evidence completes the method.
rubric.description: State the testing and concluding steps.
rubric.how: Include testing, data analysis, and a conclusion.

modelAnswer: Ask a question and form a hypothesis.
Make a prediction and test it through investigation or experimentation.
Collect and analyse data, then draw a conclusion.

written.text: Q9.5. What is a hypothesis? Give an example.
written.finalAnswer: A hypothesis is a possible answer to a question that can be investigated. For example, a plant given more light will grow faster.

rubric.why: The definition identifies the role of a hypothesis.
rubric.how: Describe it as a possible answer or explanation that can be investigated.

rubric.why: A relevant example demonstrates the definition.
rubric.how: State a testable proposed answer to a question.

modelAnswer: A hypothesis is a possible answer to a question that can be investigated.
For example, a plant given more light will grow faster.

written.text: Q9.6. Distinguish between a theory and a law of Physics.
written.finalAnswer: A theory is a well-supported explanation of observations and evidence. A law describes a regular pattern or relationship in nature.

rubric.why: The distinction must state what a theory does.
rubric.how: Explain that a theory is a well-supported explanation.

rubric.why: The distinction must also state what a law describes.
rubric.how: Say that a law describes a regular pattern or relationship in nature.

modelAnswer: A theory is a well-supported explanation of observations and evidence.
A law describes a regular pattern or relationship in nature.

written.text: Q9.8. What is falsifiability concept? How is it important?
written.finalAnswer: Falsifiability means that a scientific idea can be tested in a way that could show it to be wrong. It is important because a claim that cannot possibly be tested or disproved cannot be evaluated scientifically.

rubric.why: The definition must include the possibility of disproving a claim.
rubric.how: State that an idea can be tested and could be shown wrong.

rubric.why: The answer must explain why this property matters to science.
rubric.how: Connect testability to judging scientific claims using evidence.

modelAnswer: Falsifiability means that a scientific idea can be tested in a way that could show it to be wrong.
It is important because a claim that cannot possibly be tested or disproved cannot be evaluated scientifically.

written.text: Q9.1. Is the theory of science an ultimate truth? Describe briefly.
written.finalAnswer: No. A scientific theory is a well-supported explanation based on available evidence, but it is not an ultimate truth. New evidence may lead scientists to modify or reject it.

rubric.why: The response must answer the question directly.
rubric.how: State that a scientific theory is not an ultimate truth.

rubric.why: A theory should be described as evidence-based, not a guess.
rubric.how: Say that it is a well-supported explanation based on evidence.

rubric.why: Scientific explanations remain open to revision.
rubric.how: Mention that new evidence can require modification.

rubric.why: A full answer recognises that a theory may be modified or rejected.
rubric.how: Conclude that a theory can be rejected or modified.

modelAnswer: No, a scientific theory is not an ultimate truth.
It is a well-supported explanation based on available evidence.
New evidence may require scientists to modify the theory.
If evidence contradicts it, the theory may be rejected.

written.text: Q9.2. Do you think that the existing laws of nature may need a change in future? Describe briefly.
written.finalAnswer: Yes. A law describes a regular pattern supported by observations and evidence available at the time. New evidence or improved measurements may require scientists to revise how a law is stated or understood.

rubric.why: The response must take a clear position.
rubric.how: Answer yes and indicate that revision may be needed.

rubric.why: The answer should show what a law represents.
rubric.how: Say that it describes a regular pattern in nature.

rubric.why: A change must be linked to a scientific reason.
rubric.description: Give the reason for possible revision.
rubric.how: Mention new evidence or more accurate measurements.

rubric.why: The conclusion explains what scientists may need to do.
rubric.how: Explain that a law's statement or understanding may be revised.

modelAnswer: Yes, existing laws of nature may need revision in the future.
A law describes a regular pattern supported by observations and evidence.
New evidence or improved measurements may reveal limits in the present description.
Scientists may then revise how the law is stated or understood.

written.text: Q9.4. Describe when a theory is rejected or needs its modification.
written.finalAnswer: A theory needs modification when new observations or experimental results do not agree with part of its explanation. It is rejected when reliable evidence repeatedly contradicts its main claims and a better explanation accounts for the evidence.

rubric.why: The answer must identify the evidence that prompts reconsideration.
rubric.how: Mention observations or experimental results.

rubric.why: Conflicting evidence is the reason a theory is reconsidered.
rubric.how: Say that the evidence conflicts with the theory's explanation.

rubric.why: Some conflicts may be resolved by changing part of the explanation.
rubric.how: Explain that a theory is modified when part of it needs correction.

rubric.why: A complete answer distinguishes rejection from modification.
rubric.how: Explain that persistent contradiction of its main claims can lead to rejection.

modelAnswer: A theory needs modification when new observations or experimental results do not agree with part of its explanation.
Scientists test the theory against further evidence.
If only part of the explanation conflicts with the evidence, that part may be modified.
If reliable evidence repeatedly contradicts its main claims, the theory may be rejected.

written.text: Q9.5. Comment on the statement. “A theory capable of being proved right but not being proved wrong is not a scientific theory”.
written.finalAnswer: The statement is correct. A scientific theory must be falsifiable: evidence and tests must be capable of showing that it is wrong. If no possible test could disprove it, it cannot be evaluated scientifically.

rubric.why: The response must evaluate the statement.
rubric.how: State that the statement is correct or that you agree.

rubric.why: Falsifiability is the central concept in the statement.
rubric.how: Explain that a scientific theory must be capable of being tested and shown wrong.

rubric.why: Scientific ideas are assessed through testable evidence.
rubric.how: Mention evidence or tests that could challenge the theory.

rubric.why: The conclusion states why non-falsifiable claims are not scientific theories.
rubric.how: Explain that an idea with no possible disproof cannot be evaluated scientifically.

modelAnswer: The statement is correct.
A scientific theory must be falsifiable.
This means evidence and tests must be capable of showing that the theory is wrong.
If no possible test could disprove it, it cannot be evaluated scientifically.

written.text: Q9.7. If a hypothesis is not testable, is the hypothesis wrong? Explain.
written.finalAnswer: No. An untestable hypothesis is not automatically wrong; it simply cannot be checked using an investigation at present. It also cannot be confirmed scientifically without a way to test it.

rubric.why: The answer must distinguish lack of testing from proof of falsity.
rubric.how: State that an untestable hypothesis is not necessarily wrong.

rubric.why: This explains the practical issue with an untestable hypothesis.
rubric.how: Say that it cannot currently be checked by investigation.

rubric.why: The response must avoid treating lack of evidence as contrary evidence.
rubric.how: Explain that being untestable does not prove the hypothesis false.

rubric.why: A complete explanation also recognises that untestable claims cannot be scientifically confirmed.
rubric.how: Explain that scientific confirmation requires a test and evidence.

modelAnswer: No, an untestable hypothesis is not automatically wrong.
It means that it cannot be checked using an investigation at present.
The lack of a test does not prove the hypothesis false.
However, it cannot be confirmed scientifically without a way to test it.

written.text: Q9.3. What is scientific method? Describe its main steps with examples.
written.finalAnswer: The scientific method is an organized way of investigating questions using evidence. For example, to investigate whether more light helps a plant grow, ask the question, form the hypothesis that more light leads to faster growth, predict the result, test plants under different light conditions, collect and analyse growth data, and draw a conclusion.

rubric.why: This defines the scientific method.
rubric.how: Describe it as an organized investigation using evidence.

rubric.why: The early stages establish what is being tested.
rubric.how: Include a question, hypothesis, and prediction.

rubric.why: An investigation must test the idea and gather evidence.
rubric.how: Explain how the prediction is tested and data collected.

rubric.why: The method uses the evidence to reach a reasoned outcome.
rubric.how: Analyse the data and state a conclusion linked to the example.

modelAnswer: The scientific method is an organized way of investigating questions using evidence.
For example, ask: does more light help a plant grow?
Form a hypothesis that a plant receiving more light will grow faster, and predict the result.
Test plants under different light conditions, collect and analyse growth data, and draw a conclusion.

written.text: Q9.4. Differentiate the terms, science, technology and engineering with examples.
written.finalAnswer: Science builds knowledge about the natural world through investigation; for example, Physics explains how heat moves. Technology applies knowledge to make useful tools or processes; for example, an air conditioner uses ideas about heat transfer. Engineering uses scientific and mathematical knowledge to design and build solutions; for example, engineers design an air-conditioning system.

rubric.why: Science is distinguished by building knowledge through inquiry.
rubric.how: State that science investigates the natural world to build knowledge.

rubric.why: Technology applies knowledge for practical use.
rubric.how: Describe it as applying knowledge to make useful tools or processes.

rubric.why: Engineering uses knowledge to design and construct solutions.
rubric.how: Mention designing or building practical solutions.

rubric.why: Examples help distinguish the three terms clearly.
rubric.how: Provide examples linked to science, technology, and engineering.

modelAnswer: Science builds knowledge about the natural world through investigation; for example, Physics explains how heat moves.
Technology applies knowledge to make useful tools or processes; for example, an air conditioner uses ideas about heat transfer.
Engineering uses scientific and mathematical knowledge to design and build solutions.
For example, engineers design an air-conditioning system.

written.text: Q9.5. What is the scope of Physics in everyday life? Give some examples.
written.finalAnswer: Physics has a wide scope in everyday life because its principles are used in transport, communication, household appliances, and medicine. For example, thermodynamics is used in refrigeration and air conditioning, electromagnetism in electrical devices, and optics in lenses.

rubric.why: The answer should indicate that Physics is widely applied.
rubric.how: Say that Physics has applications across everyday life.

rubric.why: Application areas show the breadth of the subject.
rubric.how: Give at least two areas where Physics is used.

rubric.why: A specific physics principle linked to an application supports the answer.
rubric.how: Connect thermodynamics with refrigeration or air conditioning.

rubric.why: Additional examples demonstrate breadth and understanding.
rubric.how: Link a Physics branch or principle to an everyday use.

modelAnswer: Physics has a wide scope in everyday life.
Its principles are used in transport, communication, household appliances, and medicine.
Thermodynamics is used in refrigeration and air conditioning.
Electromagnetism is used in electrical devices, while optics is used in lenses.

examTips: Short questions often ask for definitions, lists, or a distinction, such as hypothesis, theory, and law; write the key definition first.

For a scientific-method question, write the stages in order and connect them to one clear example.
For comparison questions on science, technology, and engineering, define each term separately and give a suitable example for each.

steps.why: An investigation begins by identifying a question that can be examined.
steps.text: Question: Does more light help a plant grow faster?

steps.why: A hypothesis gives a possible answer that can be investigated.
steps.text: Hypothesis: A plant receiving more light will grow faster.

steps.why: A prediction states the expected result if the hypothesis is correct.
steps.text: Prediction: Plants given more light will show more growth over the same period.

steps.why: A fair test gives evidence that can be compared.
steps.text: Test: Keep similar plants under different amounts of light while keeping other conditions the same.

steps.why: Measurements provide the data needed to evaluate the prediction.
steps.text: Data: Record each plant's growth over the same period.

steps.why: The conclusion must follow from the collected evidence.
steps.text: Conclusion: Compare the growth data to decide whether it supports the hypothesis.

explain.title: Science and its groups
explain.body: Science is a way of studying the natural world by using investigation and evidence. Its two broad groups are physical science and life science. Physics belongs to physical science.

explain.title: Physics and its branches
explain.body: Physics studies matter, energy, and their interactions. Its branches include mechanics, heat, sound, light, and electricity and magnetism. These ideas support many technologies and engineering applications.

explain.title: Scientific method
explain.body: Scientists ask questions, propose hypotheses, make predictions, test ideas, collect and analyse data, and draw conclusions. Investigations may use observation, experimentation, or research.

explain.title: Theories, laws, and evidence
explain.body: A theory is an evidence-supported explanation; a law describes a regular pattern in nature. Neither should be treated as beyond examination: new evidence can lead scientists to revise ideas.

explain.title: Falsifiability and collaboration
explain.body: A scientific claim must be open to testing that could show it to be wrong. Complex questions may involve several fields, so researchers with different kinds of scientific knowledge collaborate.

mistakes: Do not describe a hypothesis as a proven fact; it is a possible answer that needs investigation.
Do not say that a theory is simply a guess; a scientific theory is supported by evidence.
Do not confuse a theory with a law: a theory explains, while a law describes a regular pattern.
Do not claim that one confirming result proves a prediction is always correct; further testing is needed.
Do not conclude that an untestable hypothesis is automatically false; it cannot be scientifically checked without a test.
When describing the scientific method, do not leave out testing, data analysis, or the conclusion.
